shows.title: John Giorno: LIFE IS A KILLER
shows.description:
John Giorno spent his career arguing that a poem shouldn't end on the page, and this show — his first solo exhibition in Mexico City — makes that argument physically real. Giant "Poem Paintings" render phrases like LIFE IS A KILLER and SPACE FORGETS YOU as bold black-and-white or rainbow-colored wall text, treating language as a purely visual, almost Pop-graphic material rather than something to be read quietly. The work grew out of Giorno's tight circle with Allen Ginsberg, William Burroughs, and Andy Warhol, and his lifelong Tibetan Buddhist practice runs underneath all of it as a belief that repetition and scale can transform meaning.

Alongside the paintings are silkscreen prints from the late 1960s and early '70s built from newspaper headlines and personal ads, several using Giorno's double-column format meant to be read aloud. The show's center of gravity, though, is a live performance stage with a suspended microphone and four turntables (developed with longtime collaborator Rirkrit Tiravanija) playing records from Giorno Poetry Systems, the nonprofit he founded in 1965 — visitors can select and layer up to four LPs at once, turning the gallery into an unpredictable, self-generated soundscape.

The project room adds Tiravanija's ten-hour film of Giorno performing at his home on the Bowery, and the gallery bookstore holds an archive of ephemera from Dial-A-Poem and Giorno Poetry Systems. Taken together, it's less a conventional retrospective than an attempt to keep Giorno's core idea alive: that poetry only really exists in the room, moving between people.

venue.name: kurimanzutto
venue.address: C. Gobernador Rafael Rebollar 94, San Miguel Chapultepec I Sección, Miguel Hidalgo

shows.title: Sculptural Evocations
shows.description:
This is a late-career survey of Manuel Felguérez, one of the architects of geometric abstraction in postwar Mexico, built from sculptures and paintings drawn from the artist's own estate and made between the 1980s and 2015. Rather than a chronological retrospective, the gallery has organized the show around three distinct bodies of sculptural work: polychrome metal maquettes originally conceived as studies for public monuments (in the lineage of his landmark Puerta 1808), a group of denser, more organic bronzes from the 1990s depicting owls, cats, and other creatures, and small carved-wood models for pieces he later scaled up in painted iron. A run of five oil paintings from the 1980s, worked with heavy impasto in earthy ochres and grays, rounds out the presentation.

Felguérez trained in Europe in the 1940s before returning to Mexico and, by the 1970s, distilling his painting into the pared-down geometry associated with La Máquina Estética — the body of work that made him central to the so-called geometrismo movement here. What's compelling about this selection is watching that rigor loosen over time: the later bronzes trade hard angles for rounded, almost bodily volumes, showing an artist still restlessly moving between painting and sculpture into his final years.

For anyone interested in Mexican modernism beyond the muralists, this is a rare chance to see maquette-scale versions of public sculptures alongside the paintings that ran parallel to them — material that spent years in the artist's own house and studio before this showing.

venue.name: Proyectos Monclova
venue.address: Calle Lamartine 415, Polanco

shows.title: Interrupted Images
shows.description:
Guillermo García Cruz's Interrupted Images brings together a body of new work that treats the picture plane as something unstable — surfaces that seem to glitch, fold, or break mid-frame rather than resolve into a single coherent image. Judging from the installation views, the gallery has hung the work salon-style across several walls, with pieces ranging from tightly cropped, almost photographic compositions to more abstracted, textural canvases, suggesting an artist working across media and scale rather than repeating a single formula.

The title points to a preoccupation running through the show: images caught in the act of falling apart or being reassembled, as if the artist is asking how much information a picture can lose before it stops functioning as one. That question feels current for a moment saturated with screenshots, compression artifacts, and algorithmic image-making, though García Cruz's handling stays resolutely physical and handmade rather than didactic about technology.

It's a tightly focused solo presentation, and a good opportunity to see a younger name in the Proyectos Monclova roster developing ideas about perception and image-breakdown that sit well alongside the gallery's other current show of Manuel Felguérez's studio-bound formal experiments.

venue.name: Proyectos Monclova
venue.address: Calle Lamartine 415, Polanco

shows.title: No es un poema, aunque soñemos muchas cosas
shows.artist: Lagartijas Tiradas al Sol (curators), with Abril Ramos Xochiteotzin, Bagus Pandega, Dayanita Singh, Eduardo Pizarro, Isabel Yáñez, Jo Ractliffe, Luisa Pardo, Lázaro Gabino Rodríguez, Mario García Torres, Matthew Krishanu, Mirosław Bałka, Nereyda López, Nicolás Pereda, Olga de Amaral, Pedro Pizarro, Soumya Sankar Bose
shows.description:
Lagartijas Tiradas al Sol, the Mexico City theater and performance collective founded in 2003, steps into a role it doesn't usually occupy: curator of a visual-art exhibition. Rather than staging a play, the group has assembled works by a wide, deliberately mismatched set of artists — Dayanita Singh's photographs, Olga de Amaral's woven fiber works, Mirosław Bałka's sculpture, Mario García Torres's conceptual pieces, alongside painting, video and installation by Bagus Pandega, Jo Ractliffe, Matthew Krishanu, Soumya Sankar Bose and others — around the idea that art's defining quality is movement rather than any fixed meaning or medium.

Because the collective's own practice is built on performance, the show doesn't sit still: it unfolds through a running program of live pieces staged inside the gallery across the eight-week run, including Luisa Pardo's "Epifanía Sideral" at the opening, Abril Ramos Xochiteotzin's "Pornita" in October, and Isabel Yáñez's "Había bruma y hacía frío" toward the close, plus a public conversation with an invited artist. The exhibition doubles as a kind of theater set that keeps getting re-activated, so the gallery looks different depending on when you visit.

The show opens during GAMA Week, Mexico City's citywide gallery walk, which makes it a natural entry point into the Roma Norte gallery circuit this month. Its premise — treating the white cube as a stage rather than a static display — is unusual enough among the neighborhood's painting- and object-heavy programming to make it worth a special trip.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 3, 12–8pm, with opening performance "Epifanía Sideral" by Luisa Pardo at 7pm

venue.name: Galerie Nordenhake Mexico City
venue.address: Monterrey 65, Roma Nte., Cuauhtémoc, 06700 Ciudad de México

shows.title: Abstract Stone
shows.description:
César Paternosto has spent six decades pushing at the edges of geometric abstraction, literally — his signature move, developed after years in New York's conceptualist circles, was to paint on the sides of canvases and let color spill around the frame, undermining the idea that a painting's action only happens on its front face. This survey pulls together work spanning from the late 1960s to the 2020s, tracing how that idea evolved from his early minimalist canvases into denser, more archaic-feeling compositions.

The pivot point in the show is Paternosto's research trips to Andean sites in the late 1970s, which led him to argue, in his book "The Stone and the Thread," that pre-Columbian textile and architectural abstraction anticipated much of what modernist painting later claimed as its own invention. That argument shapes everything here: acrylic and marble-dust canvases with the chromatic bands and lateral markings that became his signature, wood constructions, and watercolor-pencil works that treat line and color as almost archaeological artifacts.

It's a rare chance to see an artist who spent decades working between Argentina, New York, and Spain, and whose central thesis — that abstraction has deep American roots predating European modernism — remains a genuinely useful provocation for how we think about twentieth-century painting.

venue.name: Galería RGR
venue.address: Gral. Antonio León 48, San Miguel Chapultepec

shows.title: Toledo + Hendrix
shows.description:
This exhibition puts two towering figures of Mexican graphic art side by side for the first time: Francisco Toledo (1940–2019), the Oaxacan painter and ceramicist obsessed with fantastical zoological imagery, and Jan Hendrix, the Dutch-born, Mexico-based artist whose landscapes and botanical studies have made him one of the country's most distinctive adopted voices. The two met in 1976 and stayed close for decades, crossing paths through shared print projects like the IAGO and the magazine El Alcaraván.

The show leans on that history of collaboration rather than staging a simple two-artist survey. Toledo's ceramic work — vessels, fantastical creatures, and self-referential imagery dealing with memory, life and death — sits opposite Hendrix's tapestries, etchings, and drawings of dense plant life and landscape. Where Hendrix is oriented toward the vegetal world as observed fact, Toledo bends nature toward myth and grief; curator Cuauhtémoc Medina frames the pairing as a way of surfacing affinities between the two that were never presented together in their lifetimes.

Given GAM's own history as the gallery that gave Hendrix his early Mexican exposure, this is as much a piece of institutional memory as it is a fresh curatorial pairing — a chance to see the graphic language shared by two artists whose reputations mostly developed on separate tracks.

venue.name: Galería de Arte Mexicano (GAM)
venue.address: C. Gobernador Rafael Rebollar 43, San Miguel Chapultepec I Sección, Miguel Hidalgo

shows.title: Bruma Láctea
shows.description:
Michelle Sitton made this body of paintings between giving birth and the months of postpartum that followed, and the show reads as a direct record of that stretch of time rather than a metaphor for it. Figures dissolve and reassemble across clouds, roots, spirals, and half-human, half-animal forms — an iconography Sitton has built specifically to describe how the body, identity, and self-perception shift with new motherhood.

Curated by Julián Madero Islas for GAM's sala:GAM project space, the paintings mix the everyday texture of early parenthood with more fantastical imagery — angels, dragons, children — treating maternal experience as a subject with real pictorial range rather than a single register of tenderness or exhaustion. Sitton, born in Mexico City in 1995, has built her practice around the body and questions of identity, and this show marks a clear pivot point in that ongoing work.

It's a smaller, more intimate counterpart to the historical pairing showing concurrently in GAM's main galleries, and worth seeing as a snapshot of how a younger Mexican painter is handling a subject — pregnancy and postpartum — that gets surprisingly little serious gallery treatment.

venue.name: Galería de Arte Mexicano (GAM)
venue.address: C. Gobernador Rafael Rebollar 43, San Miguel Chapultepec I Sección, Miguel Hidalgo

shows.title: Selva color del tiempo
shows.description:
José Gamarra's first solo exhibition in Mexico gathers six decades of painting, from ink drawings of the 1960s to a large new canvas finished this year, and it announces Mariane Ibrahim's continued investment in Latin American modernist and postwar figures alongside its contemporary roster. Gamarra, born in Uruguay in 1934 and based in Paris since the 1960s, built his reputation on a singular subject: a version of the American tropical forest that is invented rather than observed, assembled from historical and literary references — Frans Post's colonial landscapes, Horacio Quiroga's fiction, Lévi-Strauss's ethnography — rather than firsthand experience of the Amazon.

Within that invented jungle, Gamarra layers conquistadors, Indigenous figures, helicopters, extraction machinery and wildlife into a single pictorial space where different eras of American history coexist rather than following one another in sequence. The effect, built up over paintings spanning 1966 to 2026, treats the forest as an archive of conquest, colonization and resource extraction rather than as backdrop or scenery — a way of reading continental history through landscape painting instead of narrative.

The show's title comes from a text the writer and theorist Édouard Glissant — a close friend and longtime interlocutor of Gamarra's — wrote for the artist's 1985 Paris exhibition, and the curatorial framing leans on Glissant's thinking about relation to unpack what the forest is doing in this work. For a gallery best known internationally for contemporary photography and figuration, mounting a historical survey of a Latin American painter in his nineties is a notable curatorial turn, and it's a rare chance to see this body of work outside Europe.

venue.name: Mariane Ibrahim
venue.address: Río Pánuco 36, Col. Renacimiento, Cuauhtémoc, 06500 Ciudad de México

shows.title: Aguacero
shows.description:
Andrew Holmquist's second solo show with Karen Huber turns its attention squarely on Mexico City, using it as the setting for paintings and ceramic sculptures built around fleeting, half-remembered moments. The anchor piece, a large interior bar scene, warps the room's geometry into something closer to a rollercoaster — countertops crowded with the debris of a good night, a bartender pouring a glowing drink, a mirror pushing the perspective further off its axis. It's maximalist, funny, and a little dizzying by design.

Elsewhere the tone cools into a set of "bather" paintings, quieter scenes of men at rest near water where the figures dissolve toward abstraction, less bodies than states of unburdened motion. A parallel series of ceramic sculptures, made at Taller El Camaleón, translates that same fluid brushwork into three dimensions — boat-like forms that carry Holmquist's loose, wet-on-wet painting logic into clay and glaze.

Smaller genre scenes — a banana vendor, a face-painting stand, a man framed against rain-streaked windows over a crosswalk — supply the show's title: the sudden, drenching downpours of the capital's rainy season, and by extension the abrupt shifts in mood and light that Holmquist treats as the real subject of the work. Painted in muted pinks and cool mauves, these scenes read as a love letter to a city that keeps surprising him.

venue.name: Galería Karen Huber
venue.address: Bucareli 120, Colonia Juárez/Centro, Cuauhtémoc, 06040 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: ¡Vé a pintar! (Go Paint!)
shows.description:
Cecilia Granara's first solo show in Mexico City takes its title from a phrase that reads as both command and mantra: go paint, come back to yourself, connect to something beyond language. The paintings work through a compact, symbolically loaded palette — Persian blue, Eden green, red-orange bodies — and recurring figures who mirror, touch, and transmit breath or energy to one another, turning the gallery into something like a circuit.

Granara paints herself literally, from digestive system to nervous system, alongside animals, candles, and light sources that recur as connective tissue between images: birds arriving as if in aid, turtles and flames appearing and receding across canvases. The show's visual language nods openly to predecessors — Matisse's flattened color fields, Kahlo's doubled selves, Louise Bourgeois's anatomical drawing — but its clearest lineage, as the accompanying text by Susana Vargas Cervantes argues, runs through women painters like Hilma af Klint, Agnes Pelton, and Emma Kunz, who treated painting as a channel to the unseen rather than simply a way of picturing the world.

It's a show more interested in being felt than decoded, and its own wall text asks viewers to sit with that discomfort — to receive the paintings before rushing to interpret them.

venue.name: Galería Karen Huber
venue.address: Bucareli 120, Colonia Juárez/Centro, Cuauhtémoc, 06040 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: el motion
shows.artist: Jihyoung Han, Miguel Calderón, Bárbara Sánchez-Kane, Empire Libre
shows.description:
Curated by Aureliano Alvarado Faesler, el motion turns Galería Mascota into what its own curatorial text calls a shrine-like dwelling — a group show built around the idea that contemporary life has become sensorially overloaded to the point of numbness, and that art might still offer a way to reactivate feeling without resorting to false unity or spectacle. A rope strung across the gallery guides visitors' movement through the space, a wry, un-cooperative substitute for Ariadne's thread that offers no promised exit from the show's tangle of ideas.

The four artists in the show approach that premise from different angles. Jihyoung Han paints degraded internet ephemera — memes, fads, algorithmic debris — as if they were haunted icons, charged with residual meaning despite their disposability. Miguel Calderón photographs Buddhist devotional sculptures found incongruously parked in mattress showrooms, a deadpan gag about how commercial space swallows and neutralizes ritual objects. Bárbara Sánchez-Kane works her ongoing engagement with masculinity, queerness, and Catholic iconography into objects that carry a relic-like charge without being devotional in any straightforward sense. Empire Libre contributes a bronze sculpture developed from a 17th-century German ornamental engraving, reworked through CNC machining and digital modeling into a hybrid object caught between craft history and contemporary fabrication.

It's a dense, theory-forward premise — the accompanying essay leans on Walter Benjamin, Fredric Jameson, and the concept of "cosmotechnics" — but the works themselves stay grounded in concrete, often funny material: mattress-store Buddhas, CNC-milled bronze, meme paintings. Worth seeing for viewers interested in how younger Mexico City and international artists are handling the collision of digital culture, religious imagery, and craft.

venue.name: Galería Mascota
venue.address: Valladolid 33, Roma Nte., Cuauhtémoc, 06700 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Hipervínculos: Alejandro Cartagena 2005-2026
shows.description:
Patricia Conde Galería opens its fall season with a two-decade survey of Alejandro Cartagena, the Monterrey-based photographer best known for turning an ordinary commuter highway into a lens on Mexican inequality. "Hipervínculos" — hyperlinks — is the organizing idea: rather than a strict chronology, the show is built as a web of connections between bodies of work made between 2005 and 2026, letting recurring themes of housing, labor, and suburban sprawl surface across very different series.

Cartagena made his name with Carpoolers, the aerial-view photographs of construction workers riding in the open beds of pickup trucks along Monterrey's Highway 85 — images that turned an overlooked daily commute into a quietly devastating portrait of who builds the city and who gets to live in it. That project sits within a wider practice, Suburbia Mexicana, that has tracked the raw edges of Mexico's exploding suburban developments for years, and his photographs are held by institutions from SFMOMA to the National Gallery of Art.

A twenty-year retrospective from a gallery that has represented Cartagena's work for museum acquisitions is a rare chance to see the arc of a single photographic project turn into a career-long argument about urbanization, labor, and visibility, all under one roof in the neighborhood where so much of the city's contemporary art now lives.

venue.name: Patricia Conde Galería
venue.address: Calle Gral. Juan Cano 68, San Miguel Chapultepec I Sección, Miguel Hidalgo, 11850 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Quiet Emergence
shows.description:
Saenger Galería's Main Room hosts the first solo exhibition in the Americas by Japanese painter Mio Yamato, an artist whose work turns the involuntary rhythms of the body — pulse, breath, tremor — into abstract mark-making. Thirty-seven pieces trace three overlapping series: the dot-and-line paintings in which an unsteady hand, guided only by its own pulse, builds up fields of red marks over time like a diary; a group of works made by blowing soap-and-acrylic bubbles onto canvas so that breath itself determines the final composition; and glass-based pieces that mimic microscope slides, treating paint as if it were a sample of the artist's own blood.

What ties the three bodies of work together is Yamato's refusal of total control — each series depends on some bodily or physical process (a shaking hand, the length of an exhale, the pooling of a fluid) to finish the image, so the paintings read less as designed compositions than as records of physiological time passing. It's a quiet, exacting kind of abstraction, closer to a science of the involuntary than to gestural expressionism.

For a gallery that has built its program around material experimentation in painting, bringing over an artist whose entire practice hinges on ceding control to the body is a sharp curatorial move, and this show is worth the trip to Tacubaya for anyone interested in where process-based painting can still go.

venue.name: Saenger Galería
venue.address: Manuel Dublán 33, Tacubaya, Miguel Hidalgo, 11870 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Soplar una nube de polvo en la cara (Blowing a Cloud of Dust in the Face)
shows.description:
In Saenger Galería's Project Room, stage director and painter Temoc Camacho stages his first solo show in Mexico City as a pictorial installation rather than a simple hang of canvases — a room built around a mise en abyme of a solitary figure delivering a monologue to an unseen, unidentified audience. The paintings that make up the piece are drawn from images stored in the artist's own phone gallery: pictures kept but rarely looked at, caught between circulation and deletion.

Camacho, a Guadalajara-born artist whose theatrical background shows in how deliberately the installation is staged, uses the show to think through what constant digital archiving does to memory and identity — the cache, the trash bin, the cloud reframed as psychological terrain rather than technical infrastructure. It's a dense, literary premise (the wall text draws on Baudelaire's Paris Spleen and Walter Benjamin's Angel of History alongside the artist's own commentary), but the paintings themselves stay grounded in a single recurring image: an anonymous seated figure, watched by equally anonymous others.

It's a smaller, more introverted counterpart to the gallery's Main Room show, and worth seeing as a study in how a painter trained for the stage handles the psychological weight of images we all quietly hoard and never look at again.

venue.name: Saenger Galería
venue.address: Manuel Dublán 33, Tacubaya, Miguel Hidalgo, 11870 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Junta de Verano
shows.description:
Pedro&Juana, the Mexico City studio founded by Ana Paula Ruiz Galindo and Mecky Reuss, take over AGO Projects' Reforma space with a scenography built from their own working logic: a meeting room at the center, ringed by a garden. The installation folds furniture, lighting, and object-design pieces from the wider AGO roster into the studio's own vocabulary, staging a semi-transparent refuge — part office, part patio — where visitors can sit out Mexico City's rainy summer afternoons.

Centerpiece of the show is La Patona, a communal table around which the rest of the installation orbits, alongside the Margarito bookshelf displaying objects contributed by friends of the gallery. Outside this inner room, an inverted courtyard reverses the usual relationship between interior and exterior: the portico becomes a planted garden of potted greenery, lamps, and chairs, turning the gallery's architecture inside out.

Pedro&Juana have built a design practice on exactly this kind of playful spatial inversion — domestic interiors turned inside out, furniture that behaves like architecture — and this show functions as a compact survey of that sensibility rather than a single object or line. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about Mexico City's design-forward gallery scene, where the line between furniture, sculpture, and installation is treated as beside the point.

venue.name: AGO Projects
venue.address: Av. P.º de la Reforma 382, Juárez, Cuauhtémoc, 06600 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Ex Soup, Stirring the Broth: Recipes for Chewing and Digesting the City
shows.description:
MASA's summer show turns its 19th-century San Miguel Chapultepec house into something between a kitchen and a city block, using the metaphor of soup — a dish made by combining disparate, often leftover ingredients into one simmering whole — to talk about how a metropolis like Mexico City absorbs and remakes everything thrown into it. Under the collective banner "Ex Soup," the exhibition brings together sculptural and design objects that read as utensils, vessels, and furniture at once, blurring MASA's usual line between art and functional design.

The installation photographs show a loose, almost domestic arrangement of pieces across the gallery's rooms and courtyard: cast and welded forms that suggest cookware and communal seating, materials left visibly worked and reworked, and objects that invite handling rather than pure contemplation. The "recipes" of the title aren't literal instructions so much as a framework for thinking about assimilation, digestion, and reuse — apt themes for a gallery whose stock in trade is Mexican material culture and craft.

It's a lighter, more playful outing than some of MASA's monographic shows, closer in spirit to its group exhibitions like Collective/Collectible, and worth a visit for anyone curious about how the city's design scene metabolizes everyday material into something strange and specific.

venue.name: MASA
venue.address: Joaquín A. Pérez 6, San Miguel Chapultepec I Sección, Miguel Hidalgo, 11850 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Ni mudo ni vacío (Neither Mute Nor Empty)
shows.dates_note: Venue's current exhibitions index lists this show as "10 Jul- 15 sept 2026"; the show's own page text still shows an earlier closing date of "Agosto 29, 2026" — using the exhibitions index as the more current source since today falls within its window.
shows.description:
Ulrik López Medel's solo show is built around the residue of use — the glitter that lingers in a pocket long after carnival season, the ghost outline left by a peeled sticker, the worn grip of a tool. Working across assemblage, casting, cartonería, watercolor and metal embossing, López Medel treats these throwaway traces as small talismans, akin to the Yoruba ààlè: makeshift objects assembled from scraps and rags that are believed to protect or warn precisely because of, not despite, their humble materials.

The show gathers a deliberately un-unified body of work rather than a single series: palm seeds cast in wax and turned into ornate objects, a food grater's texture worked into a sculpted head referencing the Yoruba concept of Ori (consciousness), and a paper sculpture built like a Japanese akari lamp that quietly commemorates a public-transport driver's retirement. The connecting thread is López Medel's method — noticing the "ghosts of use" embedded in ordinary forms and giving them a second, stranger life as objects.

It's a modest-looking but conceptually dense show, more interested in material intuition than in a tidy thesis, and it rewards close looking at the individual pieces rather than a quick read of the room.

venue.name: General Expenses
venue.address: Medellín 263, Roma Sur, Cuauhtémoc, 06760 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: Encontrar se
shows.artist: Luisa Bordas, Ana Teresa Fierro, Alex Hochstrasser, Anette Kuhn, Aurora Noreña, ORLAN, Erandine de Saint Phalle, Elisabeth Strebel
shows.description:
Encontrar se ("presencia en transformación") is Terreno Baldío's special presentation for GAMA Week, bringing together eight women artists — including the French body-art pioneer ORLAN alongside Mexican and European-based artists Luisa Bordas, Ana Teresa Fierro, Alex Hochstrasser, Anette Kuhn, Aurora Noreña, Erandine de Saint Phalle and Elisabeth Strebel — around the idea of presence as something always in flux rather than fixed.

Grouping this particular set of artists together points toward a show built on the body, identity and self-transformation as recurring subjects, themes ORLAN in particular has spent a career pushing to extremes through performance and surgical self-portraiture. Shown alongside painters and sculptors working in more traditional media, the pairing suggests Terreno Baldío is using the intensity of gallery-weekend traffic to put a well-known international name in conversation with artists less often seen in Mexico City.

Because it runs for only four days during GAMA Week, this is very much a see-it-now presentation rather than a season-long show — worth prioritizing this week if you're moving through the Roma gallery circuit.

venue.name: Terreno Baldío Arte
venue.address: Orizaba 177 esq. San Luis Potosí, Roma Nte., Cuauhtémoc

shows.title: Gestos Domésticos
shows.description:
Marianna Dellekamp works in the space between drawing, sculpture, and everyday domestic ritual, and this show reads as an inventory of small, repeated gestures — folding, stacking, arranging — translated into physical and graphic form. Rather than treating housework and domestic routine as background noise, Dellekamp isolates those motions and gives them the formal weight usually reserved for more "serious" subjects.

The work fits into Le Laboratoire's long-running interest in abstraction and process-based practice, and Dellekamp's pared-down visual vocabulary — precise, understated, materially varied — sits comfortably alongside the gallery's roster of artists working across drawing, sculpture, and textile-adjacent processes.

It's a quiet, close-looking kind of show rather than a spectacle, best suited to visitors interested in how domestic labor and repetition can be reframed as a formal and conceptual subject in their own right.

venue.name: Le Laboratoire
venue.address: Calle Gral. Antonio León 56, San Miguel Chapultepec II Secc, Miguel Hidalgo

shows.title: Nexus
shows.description:
Nexus is a group painting show that leans into the word's meaning head-on: a set of connections between artists whose approaches to the medium don't obviously overlap. Shown alongside Le Laboratoire's GAMA Week programming, it functions as a survey of where painting stands within the gallery's current roster, pulled together into a single conversation rather than presented as separate solo statements.

Given the gallery's stated focus on abstraction in its broadest sense, expect a mix of approaches to surface, color, and gesture rather than a single unifying style — the kind of show designed to be walked through quickly during a gallery-hopping week like GAMA Week, but that rewards a slower look at how the individual canvases talk to each other.

venue.name: Le Laboratoire
venue.address: Calle Gral. Antonio León 56, San Miguel Chapultepec II Secc, Miguel Hidalgo

shows.title: El Trópico de Jersey (The Tropic of Jersey)
shows.description:
Emi Winter's new paintings splice together three genres that don't usually keep company: still life, landscape, and geometric abstraction. The show's engine is a simple, almost stubborn ritual — bananas set out on a studio table and painted fast, at whatever stage of ripeness they happen to be in, a nod to still-life painting's old obsession with decay and time. Those quick, visceral banana studies sit against small landscape studies painted in the nature reserves of New Jersey, the state Winter relocated to eleven years ago after leaving Oaxaca.

In the large-format paintings that give the show its charge, the two bodies of work collide: landscape studies get folded into big canvases where they share space with oversized bananas, the scale relationship flipped so the once-modest still life dominates and the landscape recedes into pattern and backdrop. The palette and structure nod to Dutch still-life painting and, closer to home, to Rufino Tamayo and María Izquierdo, while the plein-air landscape fragments carry a debt to Dr. Atl and French Impressionism.

The title is a pun with some bite: New Jersey's dense population sits beside a surprising range of protected ecosystems, and Winter's summers there are too hot and humid to paint outdoors — hence a "tropic" that isn't tropical at all, except in the sense that global trade keeps tropical fruit flowing into temperate supermarkets year-round regardless of season. It's a modest but sharp premise for a painting show, using the domestic banana as a stand-in for the reach and strangeness of globalized supply chains.

venue.name: Galería Ethra
venue.address: Londres 54, Juárez, Cuauhtémoc, 06600 Ciudad de México, CDMX

shows.title: La calle también se enmarca (The Street Also Gets Framed)
shows.description:
This is Aguafuerte's September group show devoted entirely to street photography, bringing together seventeen photographers working the sidewalks, markets, festivals and parade routes of Mexico and beyond. The catalogue ranges from Antonio Flores's pyrotechnic "toritos" (bull-shaped firework rigs) exploding in showers of red smoke, to Jair Hernández's portrait of a hooded falconer in the historic center, to Marko Eskalante's black-and-white studies of fairground vendors and Day of the Dead crowds.

What unites the work is a documentary eye trained on the unscripted texture of public life: charreada riders, ice-cream sellers, ambulant photographers, masked dancers, a cat perched in a bucket on a crumbling doorstep. Several photographers, including Etan Frías and Gloria Navor, favor a warmer, more intimate register, lingering on domestic and small-town scenes in Oaxaca's Mazateca region and rural fiestas, while others like Felipe Rubilar and Oswaldo Ramírez push toward a cooler, more graphic style of street composition.

As with most of Aguafuerte's programming, this is a selling exhibition as much as a curated statement — every print is priced and available — but the sheer range of approaches on the walls, from analog grain to saturated digital color, makes it a useful cross-section of contemporary Mexican street photography as a genre, not just a single artist's take on it.

shows.title: Tepito en la cancha
shows.description:
This is a neighborhood history show built around the deep, decades-long bond between Tepito and amateur football. Drawing on found photographs, trophies, jerseys, banners and oral testimony gathered from local players, referees and fans, the exhibition treats the barrio's street leagues and dusty courts as a living archive of identity, pride and survival.

A dedicated section is given over to Las Gardenias, a team made up of members of the neighborhood's LGBT+ community that has competed steadily in local tournaments for decades — a quietly radical footnote to Tepito's macho football culture that the curators use to complicate the usual story of who gets to play and who gets remembered.

Organized by the Galería José María Velasco, itself an INBA outpost founded specifically to bring contemporary and vernacular art to this working-class corner of the city, the show fits squarely into the gallery's long-running interest in the culture, symbols and self-representation of the Tepito community. It's less a fine-art exhibition than a communal scrapbook turned public monument — worth a visit for anyone curious about how a neighborhood tells its own history through the objects of everyday leisure.

shows.title: Encontrando el oro al final del arcoíris. Dinastía Duende 50 años
shows.description:
A half-century tribute to Dinastía Duende, one of the emblematic sound systems (sonideros) of Mexico City's popular dance-hall circuit. Sonideros are as much social infrastructure as music acts — mobile PA crews who host open-air cumbia and tropical-music dances in plazas and neighborhood streets — and Dinastía Duende has been a fixture of that world for fifty years.

The exhibition works through collective memory rather than a conventional artist's practice: photographs, flyers, sound equipment, dedications shouted out over the mic, and the testimony of dancers and organizers are assembled to show how a single sonidero became an anchor for community and family across generations of dance nights.

Presented at Galería José María Velasco, which has built its program around the popular and urban cultures of the surrounding neighborhoods, the show sits alongside the gallery's companion exhibition on Tepito's football culture as a study of how CDMX's working-class barrios generate their own institutions, loyalties and forms of collective celebration.
